questions.question: What is JavaScript?
questions.correctAnswer: An interpreted, dynamic, multi-paradigm programming language used in the browser, on the server (Node.js) and in many other environments.
wrongAnswers: A compiled, statically typed language derived from Java that runs only inside the browser's sandbox and cannot be used on servers or other environments.
A markup language used to structure web pages, similar to HTML.
A styling language that controls the layout and colors of web pages.

questions.question: What are the primitive data types?
questions.correctAnswer: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol and bigint.
wrongAnswers: string, number, boolean, object, array and function, since arrays and functions are stored by value like the other primitives.
string, int, float, char, boolean and null.
string, number, boolean, undefined, Date and RegExp.

questions.question: What is the difference between var, let and const?
questions.correctAnswer: var is function-scoped and hoisted with undefined; let and const are block-scoped; const doesn't allow reassignment.
wrongAnswers: var and let are block-scoped and can be reassigned; const is function-scoped and makes objects deeply immutable, so their properties cannot change either.
var and let are block-scoped; const is function-scoped and fully immutable.
All three are block-scoped; const prevents mutation of objects.

questions.question: What is hoisting?
questions.correctAnswer: Behavior where declarations are "lifted" to the top of the scope before execution. Functions are fully hoisted; let/const stay in the temporal dead zone.
wrongAnswers: The process in which minifiers move all variable and function declarations to the top of the file during bundling, so that the code can run in older browsers.
Moving all code to the top of the file during minification.
A feature where variables declared with let are initialized with undefined before execution.

questions.question: What is the Temporal Dead Zone?
questions.correctAnswer: The period between the start of the scope and the let/const declaration, in which accessing the variable throws a ReferenceError.
wrongAnswers: The period after a variable goes out of scope and before the garbage collector frees its memory, during which reading it returns undefined.
The time a Promise spends pending before resolving.
The delay before setTimeout(fn, 0) executes.

questions.question: What is the difference between == and ===?
questions.correctAnswer: == compares with type coercion; === compares value and type without coercion. Prefer ===.
wrongAnswers: === compares values after converting both operands to the same type, while == compares value and type strictly; prefer == for safety.
== compares object references and === compares the contents of objects deeply, so two objects with the same keys are === equal.
=== compares with type coercion; == compares value and type without coercion.

questions.question: What are falsy values?
questions.correctAnswer: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined and NaN. Everything else is truthy.
wrongAnswers: false, 0, "", null, undefined, empty arrays [] and empty objects {}. Everything else is truthy.
false, 0, "0", "false", null and undefined, because strings are converted to their meaning.
Only false and null.

questions.question: What is typeof null?
questions.correctAnswer: It returns "object", a historical bug in the language kept for compatibility.
wrongAnswers: It returns "null", since null has its own dedicated type tag in the language.
It throws a TypeError, because typeof cannot be applied to null values.
It returns "undefined".

questions.question: What is NaN?
questions.correctAnswer: "Not a Number", a numeric value resulting from invalid operations. Check it with Number.isNaN().
wrongAnswers: A special string returned when numeric parsing fails; you check for it by comparing value === "NaN" after the conversion.
An alias for null used in numeric contexts; you check for it with value === NaN, which returns true for invalid results.
An error thrown when dividing by zero.

questions.question: What is a function?
questions.correctAnswer: A reusable block of code that can receive parameters and return a value; in JS, functions are first-class values.
wrongAnswers: A special object that can only be called once and cannot be stored in variables or passed as an argument to other functions.
A block of code that always runs automatically when the page loads.
A statement that declares a class with methods.

questions.question: What is the difference between a function declaration and a function expression?
questions.correctAnswer: A declaration is fully hoisted and can be called before it is defined; an expression only exists after assignment.
wrongAnswers: A function expression is fully hoisted and can be called before it appears, while a declaration only exists after the line where it is defined runs.
A declaration cannot receive parameters or return values, while an expression can; otherwise they behave the same in every scope.
There is no difference other than syntax.

questions.question: What are arrow functions?
questions.correctAnswer: A short function syntax ((a, b) => a + b) that has no own this or arguments and inherits this from the enclosing scope.
wrongAnswers: A short syntax ((a, b) => a + b) that creates its own this bound to the caller and its own arguments object, and can be used as a constructor with new.
Functions that run asynchronously by default.
Functions that can only return objects.

questions.question: What is an object?
questions.correctAnswer: A collection of key-value pairs, the basis of most data in JavaScript.
wrongAnswers: An ordered list of values accessed only by numeric index, the basis of most data in JavaScript.
A primitive type that stores text and numbers together, compared by value.
A function that can only be created with the class keyword.

questions.question: How do you create and access object properties?
questions.correctAnswer: With literals { name: "Ana" }, accessing by obj.name or obj["name"].
wrongAnswers: With new Object("name", "Ana"), reading values only through obj.get("name") and writing through obj.set("name", value).
With array-like literals [ name: "Ana" ], accessing properties with the arrow syntax obj->name as in PHP.
With JSON strings only, accessing by obj("name").

questions.question: What is an array?
questions.correctAnswer: An ordered, indexed object for storing lists of values.
wrongAnswers: A primitive type that stores a fixed number of values of the same type, defined when it is created.
An unordered collection of unique values that ignores duplicates automatically.
A key-value structure where keys can be any type.

questions.question: What are map, filter and reduce for?
questions.correctAnswer: map transforms each item; filter selects items by a condition; reduce accumulates items into a single value.
wrongAnswers: map selects items that match a condition; filter accumulates all items into a single value; reduce transforms each item into a new one.
They mutate the original array in place and return undefined, so you must read the original array afterwards to see the result.
map sorts the array; filter removes duplicates; reduce shortens the array length.

questions.question: What is the difference between forEach and map?
questions.correctAnswer: forEach just runs something for each item and returns undefined; map returns a new transformed array.
wrongAnswers: map executes a callback for each item and returns undefined; forEach returns a new array with each item transformed by the callback.
forEach runs callbacks asynchronously in parallel, while map runs them synchronously one after another and returns a new array.
forEach can be chained and map cannot.

questions.question: How do you add and remove elements from an array?
questions.correctAnswer: push/pop at the end; unshift/shift at the start; splice at any position.
wrongAnswers: push/pop at the start of the array; unshift/shift at the end; slice inserts or removes items at any position in place.
add/remove at the end; insert/delete at the start.
Arrays are immutable, so you can only create new ones with concat.

questions.question: What is a template literal?
questions.correctAnswer: Strings with backticks that allow ${expression} interpolation and multiple lines.
wrongAnswers: Strings in single quotes that can contain HTML tags and are rendered as markup when inserted into the DOM.
A string type that cannot contain variables or expressions, used for constant messages.
A function that formats numbers as currency.

questions.question: What is destructuring?
questions.correctAnswer: Syntax for extracting values from arrays/objects into variables: const { name } = person.
wrongAnswers: Converting an object into a JSON string so it can be sent over the network.
Deleting properties from an object to free memory.
Breaking a function into smaller functions.

questions.question: What are the spread and rest operators?
questions.correctAnswer: ... expands iterables/objects (spread) or gathers remaining arguments into an array (rest).
wrongAnswers: ... creates a deep clone of nested objects (spread), or removes the last element from an array and returns it (rest).
Spread uses the ... syntax to expand values, while rest uses ** to collect the remaining arguments into an object.
... pauses a function (spread) and resumes it later (rest).

questions.question: What is the DOM?
questions.correctAnswer: A tree representation of the HTML document that JavaScript can read and manipulate.
wrongAnswers: A JavaScript library similar to jQuery that must be imported to manipulate the HTML of the page.
The browser's networking layer responsible for downloading HTML documents and their resources.
A database where the browser stores user data.

questions.question: How do you select DOM elements?
questions.correctAnswer: document.querySelector, querySelectorAll, getElementById and similar.
wrongAnswers: document.find, document.select and the $() function, which are available natively in every modern browser.
window.getElement and window.getElements, which return live arrays of matching elements.
document.query("tag") only, which returns a single element.

questions.question: What are events and how do you handle them?
questions.correctAnswer: Actions such as clicks or keypresses. You use element.addEventListener("click", handler).
wrongAnswers: Scheduled tasks that run at fixed intervals; you handle them by registering callbacks with setInterval only.
Messages pushed from the server; you handle them with element.listen("click", handler) on the target element.
Network responses; you handle them with fetch().then().

questions.question: What is null versus undefined?
questions.correctAnswer: undefined indicates the absence of an assigned value; null is an intentional absence.
wrongAnswers: null indicates that a variable was declared but never assigned, while undefined is an intentional absence set by the developer.
They are identical values, and null === undefined returns true because both represent missing data.
null is a number and undefined is a string.

questions.question: What is a scope?
questions.correctAnswer: The region of code where a variable is accessible: global, function or block.
wrongAnswers: The list of every variable declared in a program, which the engine keeps in a global table.
The lifetime of a variable in memory, measured from its creation until garbage collection.
The list of all variables declared in a program.

questions.question: What is a closure?
questions.correctAnswer: A function that "remembers" the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished.
wrongAnswers: A function that can only access global variables and constants, because local variables are destroyed when their scope ends.
A block of code that terminates a loop early and returns control to the enclosing function, similar to break.
A function that closes the browser window when called.

questions.question: What is this?
questions.correctAnswer: A reference to the execution context; its value depends on how the function is called (object, global, new, call/apply/bind).
wrongAnswers: A reference that always points to the object where the function was originally defined, no matter how or where the function is called.
A reference that always points to the global window object in browsers and to module.exports in Node.js, regardless of the call site.
A reference to the current module's exports.

questions.question: What is JSON and how do you use it?
questions.correctAnswer: A textual data format. JSON.stringify converts an object into a string and JSON.parse does the reverse.
wrongAnswers: A binary data format. JSON.parse converts an object into a string and JSON.stringify converts a string back into an object.
A JavaScript library for HTTP requests.
A database engine built into browsers.

questions.question: How does try...catch work?
questions.correctAnswer: It runs the code in try; if an error occurs, flow goes to catch; finally always runs.
wrongAnswers: It runs the catch block first and then the try block; finally only runs when an error was thrown in either of them.
It retries the code inside try automatically until it succeeds, using catch only to log each failed attempt.
It catches errors only in asynchronous callbacks.

questions.question: What are setTimeout and setInterval?
questions.correctAnswer: setTimeout runs a function once after a delay; setInterval runs it repeatedly.
wrongAnswers: setInterval runs a function once after a delay, while setTimeout runs it repeatedly at the given interval until cleared.
setTimeout pauses all JavaScript execution for the given time, and setInterval resumes execution after the pause ends.
Both run the function synchronously and block the main thread.

questions.question: What is a Promise?
questions.correctAnswer: An object representing the future result of an async operation: pending, fulfilled or rejected.
wrongAnswers: A function that always runs on a separate thread and returns its result through a shared memory buffer.
A guarantee that an operation will never fail.
A synchronous callback queue.

questions.question: What is async/await?
questions.correctAnswer: Syntax that lets you write async code sequentially; await pauses the function until the Promise resolves.
wrongAnswers: Syntax that makes async functions run in parallel threads, so await waits for a worker thread to finish its computation.
Syntax in which await blocks the entire program and the event loop until the Promise resolves, like a synchronous call.
Syntax that converts synchronous code into callbacks automatically.

questions.question: What is a callback?
questions.correctAnswer: A function passed as an argument to be called later, common in async operations and events.
wrongAnswers: A function that calls itself recursively until a base condition is reached.
A function that is executed immediately after being defined, creating a private scope.
A function that returns another function.

questions.question: What is the Event Loop?
questions.correctAnswer: A mechanism that coordinates the call stack, task queues and microtasks, enabling async operations on a single thread.
wrongAnswers: A browser feature that repeats CSS animations indefinitely and synchronizes them with the screen refresh rate.
A loop that creates a new thread for each asynchronous operation.
A for loop that iterates over DOM events.

questions.question: What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks?
questions.correctAnswer: Microtasks (Promises, queueMicrotask) run after the current task, before the next macrotask (setTimeout, events).
wrongAnswers: Macrotasks (setTimeout, events) always run before microtasks (Promises), which are processed only when the macrotask queue is empty.
Microtasks run in Web Workers and macrotasks on the main thread.
Microtasks are short functions and macrotasks are long functions.

questions.question: What is the call stack?
questions.correctAnswer: A stack that records the functions being executed; overflowing it causes Maximum call stack size exceeded.
wrongAnswers: A queue of pending Promises waiting to resolve, processed in FIFO order by the engine.
The memory area where objects and closures are allocated and later garbage collected.
The list of event listeners registered on the page.

questions.question: What are prototypes?
questions.correctAnswer: JavaScript's inheritance mechanism: objects inherit properties from their prototype, forming the prototype chain.
wrongAnswers: Draft versions of functions that the engine compiles in advance to speed up the first call.
Type declarations that describe objects, used by the engine only when TypeScript is enabled.
Draft versions of functions used during development.

questions.question: How do classes work in JS?
questions.correctAnswer: They are syntactic sugar over prototypes: class, constructor, extends, super, static methods and # private fields.
wrongAnswers: They are a separate object system, independent of prototypes, in which methods are copied into every instance as in Java.
They compile to WebAssembly modules.
They only support public fields and cannot be extended.

questions.question: How do call, apply and bind work?
questions.correctAnswer: They set this: call invokes with separate arguments, apply with an array, bind returns a new function with this fixed.
wrongAnswers: call invokes the function with an array of arguments, apply with separate arguments, and bind invokes it immediately with this fixed.
They clone a function so it can run in parallel in a different thread with its own copy of this and its arguments.
call invokes with an array, apply with separate arguments, bind invokes immediately.

questions.question: What is currying?
questions.correctAnswer: Transforming a function of several arguments into a sequence of single-argument functions: f(a)(b).
wrongAnswers: Caching the results of a function based on its arguments so repeated calls with the same input are faster.
Combining multiple functions into one, executed right to left.
Delaying function execution until the user stops typing.

questions.question: What are higher-order functions?
questions.correctAnswer: Functions that receive other functions as arguments or return them (map, filter, decorators).
wrongAnswers: Functions declared at the top level of a file, which the engine executes before any other code in the module.
Functions declared at the top of a file.
Functions with higher execution priority in the event loop.

questions.question: What is a pure function?
questions.correctAnswer: Given the same input, it always returns the same output and causes no side effects.
wrongAnswers: A function that has no parameters and only uses constants, so it can be optimized by the engine.
A function that has no parameters.
A function written without arrow syntax.

questions.question: What is immutability and how do you achieve it?
questions.correctAnswer: Not changing existing data, creating copies (spread, map, structuredClone) or using Object.freeze.
wrongAnswers: Declaring every variable with const, which makes objects and arrays deeply immutable so their contents cannot change.
Using push and splice, which create new arrays.
Storing data in localStorage so it cannot be changed.

questions.question: What is the difference between a shallow and a deep copy?
questions.correctAnswer: A shallow copy (spread, Object.assign) copies only the first level; a deep copy (structuredClone) copies recursively.
wrongAnswers: A shallow copy (structuredClone) copies only the first level of the object, while a deep copy (spread or Object.assign) copies nested objects recursively.
A shallow copy copies only primitives; a deep copy copies only functions.
They are identical; deep copy is just slower.

questions.question: What is the difference between Promise.all, allSettled, race and any?
questions.correctAnswer: all fails if one fails; allSettled waits for all and reports each result; race returns the first to settle; any the first to fulfill.
wrongAnswers: all returns the first promise that fulfills; allSettled rejects as soon as one fails; race waits for all to settle; any returns the first to settle.
all runs the promises sequentially one after another, while allSettled, race and any run them in parallel on separate threads.
all and allSettled are identical; race and any are identical.

questions.question: How do you handle errors in async/await?
questions.correctAnswer: With try/catch around the await or .catch() on the Promise.
wrongAnswers: Errors thrown inside async functions are swallowed automatically by the engine, so no explicit handling is needed.
Only with the global window.onerror handler, since try/catch does not work with await expressions.
Errors in async functions are swallowed automatically, so no handling is needed.

questions.question: What is fetch?
questions.correctAnswer: A native Promise-based API for HTTP requests; it doesn't reject on 4xx/5xx responses, so you need to check response.ok.
wrongAnswers: A native Promise-based API for HTTP requests that rejects automatically on any 4xx or 5xx response, so you only need a catch block.
A synchronous API that blocks the main thread until the HTTP response arrives, returning the parsed body directly.
A third-party library that must be installed via npm.

questions.question: What is CORS?
questions.correctAnswer: A browser security mechanism that controls cross-origin requests, configured through server headers.
wrongAnswers: A JavaScript library for making cross-domain requests.
A server-side firewall that blocks all external traffic.
A CSS feature for responsive layouts.

questions.question: What is debounce?
questions.correctAnswer: Delaying a function's execution until a period without new calls has passed (e.g., search as you type).
wrongAnswers: Limiting a function so that it runs at most once per fixed time interval, no matter how many times it is called (e.g., scroll).
Caching a function's results based on its arguments so repeated calls return immediately without recomputation.
Running a function immediately and ignoring all errors.

questions.question: What is throttle?
questions.correctAnswer: Limiting a function's execution to at most once per time interval (e.g., scroll).
wrongAnswers: Delaying a function's execution until a period without new calls has passed, so it only runs after the user stops (e.g., typing).
Slowing down outgoing network requests to save bandwidth by queuing them and sending one per second.
Running a function only once in the whole application lifetime.

questions.question: What are event bubbling and capturing?
questions.correctAnswer: Event propagation: capturing goes down from the root to the target; bubbling goes up from the target to the root. stopPropagation interrupts it.
wrongAnswers: Bubbling travels down from the root to the target and capturing travels up from the target to the root; preventDefault stops propagation.
Bubbling creates duplicate events; capturing removes them.
They describe how events are stored in memory.

questions.question: What is event delegation?
questions.correctAnswer: Registering a listener on an ancestor to handle events from many children, taking advantage of bubbling.
wrongAnswers: Registering a separate listener on every child element.
Sending events to a Web Worker for processing.
Delaying events until the page has fully loaded.

questions.question: What are generators?
questions.correctAnswer: Functions (function*) that pause with yield and return iterators, useful for lazy sequences.
wrongAnswers: Async functions (function*) that always return Promises and run their body in a separate microtask.
Functions that create new classes at runtime from a template object, used for factories.
Functions that generate random numbers.

questions.question: What are iterators and iterables?
questions.correctAnswer: An iterable implements [Symbol.iterator]; an iterator has next() returning { value, done }. Used by for...of and spread.
wrongAnswers: An iterable has a next() method returning { value, done }, and an iterator implements [Symbol.iterator]; they are used by for...in loops.
Iterators are arrays and iterables are objects.
They are only available in Node.js, not in browsers.

questions.question: What is the difference between for...in and for...of?
questions.correctAnswer: for...in iterates over enumerable keys of objects; for...of iterates over values of iterables.
wrongAnswers: for...of iterates over the enumerable keys of an object, while for...in iterates over the values of iterables such as arrays.
for...in only works with arrays and strings, while for...of only works with plain objects and their properties.
They are identical; for...of is just newer.

questions.question: What are Map and Set?
questions.correctAnswer: Map is a key-value collection with keys of any type; Set stores unique values.
wrongAnswers: Map stores unique values and ignores duplicates; Set is a key-value collection whose keys must be strings.
Map transforms arrays and Set assigns values to variables.
Both only accept strings as keys or values.

questions.question: What are WeakMap and WeakSet?
questions.correctAnswer: Collections with weak references to objects, allowing garbage collection; they are not iterable.
wrongAnswers: Smaller, faster versions of Map and Set that hold only primitive values and can be iterated with for...of.
Collections whose entries expire automatically after a configurable timeout, used as in-memory caches.
Smaller, faster versions of Map and Set that are iterable.

questions.question: What is Symbol?
questions.correctAnswer: A primitive type that creates unique identifiers, used for property keys and protocols like Symbol.iterator.
wrongAnswers: A string type used for emojis and special characters that cannot be represented with regular UTF-16 strings.
A global registry that stores every variable name used in the program so the engine can look them up faster.
An object that represents mathematical operators.

questions.question: What are optional chaining and nullish coalescing?
questions.correctAnswer: ?. accesses properties safely; ?? sets a default only for null/undefined.
wrongAnswers: ?. sets a default value for any falsy value, and ?? accesses nested properties safely without throwing errors.
?. throws a descriptive error when a property is missing, and ?? converts any value into a boolean.
Both are only available in TypeScript.

questions.question: What are Object.freeze and Object.seal for?
questions.correctAnswer: freeze makes the object immutable (shallow); seal prevents adding or removing properties but allows changing them.
wrongAnswers: seal makes the object completely immutable, while freeze only prevents adding new properties but still allows removing and changing them.
freeze makes the object and all nested objects deeply immutable, while seal encrypts its properties so they cannot be read.
Both only work in strict mode and are otherwise ignored.

questions.question: What is Proxy?
questions.correctAnswer: An object that intercepts and redefines operations (get, set, etc.) of another object.
wrongAnswers: A server that forwards HTTP requests from the browser to another origin, avoiding CORS restrictions.
A function that limits how often another function can run, similar to throttle.
A copy of an object that updates automatically.

questions.question: How does the garbage collector work?
questions.correctAnswer: It frees memory of unreachable objects, using algorithms like mark-and-sweep.
wrongAnswers: It frees memory of objects that haven't been accessed for the last 60 seconds, regardless of whether they are still referenced.
It requires developers to call delete on every object manually when it is no longer needed, otherwise memory is never released.
It only runs when the page is reloaded.

questions.question: What causes memory leaks in JS?
questions.correctAnswer: Accidental globals, listeners and timers not removed, closures retaining large data and references to removed DOM nodes.
wrongAnswers: Using const instead of let, because constants are never released by the garbage collector until the page closes.
Declaring too many functions in a single file, since every function definition reserves memory permanently.
Using const instead of let.

questions.question: What is Intl?
questions.correctAnswer: An internationalization API for formatting dates, numbers and currencies and comparing strings according to locale.
wrongAnswers: An API that automatically translates text between languages using the browser's built-in translation engine.
An API for detecting the user's IP address, country and time zone without asking for permission.
A library for handling integer math.

questions.question: How do you work with dates in JS?
questions.correctAnswer: With Date, Intl.DateTimeFormat, or libraries like date-fns/Day.js; the upcoming Temporal API will fix many limitations.
wrongAnswers: Only with Moment.js, because JavaScript has no native date support and the Date object was removed from the language.
With the native Time object, which handles time zones, formatting and arithmetic perfectly in every browser.
By storing dates as plain strings and comparing them alphabetically.

questions.question: What are CommonJS and ES Modules?
questions.correctAnswer: CommonJS uses require/module.exports (synchronous, classic Node); ES Modules use import/export (static, the language standard).
wrongAnswers: ES Modules use require/module.exports and load synchronously, while CommonJS uses import/export and is resolved statically by the language.
CommonJS is for browsers and ES Modules are only for Node.
They are two names for the same module system.

questions.question: Explain the execution order of console.log, setTimeout(0) and Promise.then.
questions.correctAnswer: Synchronous code first, then microtasks (then), and finally macrotasks (setTimeout), even with a 0 delay.
wrongAnswers: They run exactly in the order they appear in the source code, because a 0 ms delay means the callbacks execute immediately.
setTimeout(0) first, then console.log, then Promise.then.
Promise.then first, then console.log, then setTimeout.

questions.question: What is Promise.withResolvers?
questions.correctAnswer: A method that returns { promise, resolve, reject }, simplifying the creation of externally controlled promises.
wrongAnswers: A method that resolves every promise in an array at once with the same value, useful for resetting state.
A method that converts a callback-based function into a function that returns a Promise, like util.promisify.
A method that retries a promise until it resolves.

questions.question: How do you implement Promise.all from scratch?
questions.correctAnswer: Return a new Promise, iterate the promises storing results by index, resolve when the counter reaches the total and reject on the first failure.
wrongAnswers: Await each promise sequentially inside a for loop, pushing each result into an array and returning it at the end.
Wait with setTimeout for a long enough fixed delay and then read the value of each promise synchronously.
Use Promise.race in a loop until all promises resolve.

questions.question: How does prototypal inheritance work in detail?
questions.correctAnswer: When accessing a property, the engine searches the object and goes up the __proto__ chain until null; Object.create sets the prototype explicitly.
wrongAnswers: Properties are copied from the parent into each child when the object is created, so later changes to the parent never affect existing children.
The engine searches the global scope first, then the object itself, and finally the module scope, stopping at the first match.
Each object has a fixed list of parent classes defined at compile time.

questions.question: What is the difference between Object.create(null) and {}?
questions.correctAnswer: The former creates an object without a prototype (no toString, etc.), useful as a pure dictionary.
wrongAnswers: Object.create(null) returns the value null, while {} creates an empty object that inherits from Object.prototype.
{} creates an object without any prototype, while Object.create(null) inherits toString and other methods from Object.prototype.
There is no difference.

questions.question: What are property descriptors?
questions.correctAnswer: Property metadata (value, writable, enumerable, configurable, get, set), manipulated via Object.defineProperty.
wrongAnswers: JSDoc comments that describe what each property does, used by editors to show documentation on hover.
TypeScript types attached to object properties at runtime and enforced by the engine on assignment.
CSS rules applied to DOM element properties.

questions.question: What is the Reflect module?
questions.correctAnswer: An API with methods that mirror object operations, used together with Proxy.
wrongAnswers: An API for inspecting and traversing the DOM tree, returning information about elements and their styles.
A module for reading TypeScript types and decorators at runtime through reflection metadata.
An API for inspecting the DOM tree.

questions.question: What is tail call optimization in JS?
questions.correctAnswer: An optimization that reuses the call frame for calls in tail position; it is part of the spec but only supported by some engines.
wrongAnswers: An optimization implemented by every JavaScript engine that converts all recursive functions into loops automatically.
A technique that moves function calls to the end of the file so that they are executed after all declarations.
An optimization supported by all engines that removes recursion entirely.

questions.question: How do SharedArrayBuffer and Atomics work?
questions.correctAnswer: They enable shared memory between workers, with atomic operations to avoid race conditions.
wrongAnswers: They store arrays in localStorage shared between tabs.
They share arrays between server and client automatically.
They compress arrays to save memory.

questions.question: What are async iterators and for await...of?
questions.correctAnswer: Iterators that return Promises, used to consume async data streams.
wrongAnswers: Iterators that run each iteration on a separate thread so long loops don't block the main thread.
A loop that awaits all Promises in parallel and returns an array with every result at the end.
Synchronous iterators that block until all data arrives.

questions.question: How do AbortController and AbortSignal work?
questions.correctAnswer: They let you cancel async operations, such as fetch, signaling via controller.abort().
wrongAnswers: They stop the entire JavaScript program immediately, including timers and pending Promises, like process.exit.
They catch errors thrown by fetch and convert them into rejected Promises with a descriptive message.
They set a timeout for setTimeout calls.

questions.question: What is the Event Loop in Node.js vs the browser?
questions.correctAnswer: Node uses libuv with phases (timers, I/O, setImmediate, close), plus process.nextTick; the browser has task queues and rendering.
wrongAnswers: They are identical: Node.js embeds the browser's event loop from Chromium, including rendering steps and requestAnimationFrame.
The browser uses libuv with timers, I/O and close phases, while Node.js uses the rendering pipeline with animation frames.
Node runs everything synchronously; only the browser has an event loop.

questions.question: What is Tree Shaking?
questions.correctAnswer: Removing unused code during bundling, relying on static ES Modules and the absence of side effects.
wrongAnswers: Removing unused DOM nodes at runtime to reduce memory usage on pages with many elements.
Reordering the dependency tree alphabetically so that modules load in a predictable order.
Minifying variable names in the bundle.

questions.question: How does the V8 engine work?
questions.correctAnswer: It compiles JS to bytecode (Ignition) and optimizes "hot" code with JIT (TurboFan), using hidden classes and inline caching.
wrongAnswers: It interprets JavaScript line by line on every execution without any compilation or optimization, which keeps memory usage low.
It compiles all JavaScript ahead of time into native machine code before the page loads, so no JIT is involved at runtime.
It converts JavaScript into Java bytecode and runs it on the JVM.

questions.question: What are hidden classes?
questions.correctAnswer: V8 internal structures that represent the "shape" of objects; keeping the same property order improves performance.
wrongAnswers: Classes declared with the private keyword, which are hidden from other modules and cannot be imported.
CSS classes applied to elements but hidden from DevTools to protect the stylesheet from copying.
CSS classes that are applied but not visible in DevTools.

questions.question: How do you identify and fix performance bottlenecks in the browser?
questions.correctAnswer: With DevTools' Performance tab and Lighthouse, reducing main-thread work, layout thrashing and bundle size.
wrongAnswers: By wrapping expensive code in more setTimeout calls with longer delays, so the browser has time to catch up between tasks.
By adding more setTimeout calls to delay work.
By using var instead of let everywhere.

questions.question: What is layout thrashing?
questions.correctAnswer: Alternating DOM layout reads and writes that force repeated recalculations; avoid it by batching reads and writes.
wrongAnswers: Repeatedly reloading CSS files due to cache misses.
Rendering the same component twice in development.
Using too many nested flexbox containers.

questions.question: What are requestAnimationFrame and requestIdleCallback?
questions.correctAnswer: rAF runs before the next paint (animations); rIC runs during idle periods for low-priority work.
wrongAnswers: rAF runs during idle periods when the browser has nothing else to do, while rIC runs right before the next paint for animations.
rAF requests a new frame from the server for video playback, while rIC cancels pending network requests when the tab is idle.
Both run in Web Workers.

questions.question: What is a Service Worker?
questions.correctAnswer: A script that acts as a proxy between the app and the network, enabling offline caching, push notifications and PWAs.
wrongAnswers: A Web Worker with direct access to the DOM that renders parts of the page in the background.
A Node.js process on the server that handles incoming HTTP requests for the web app.
A browser extension that blocks ads.

questions.question: What is XSS and how do you prevent it?
questions.correctAnswer: Script injection into pages. Prevent it by sanitizing/escaping input, avoiding innerHTML with untrusted data and using CSP.
wrongAnswers: A cross-site request forgery attack in which a malicious site sends requests with the user's cookies; prevent it by enabling CORS on the server.
A CSS bug that breaks layouts in some browsers; prevent it by including a CSS reset and avoiding vendor prefixes.
A server overload attack; prevent it with rate limiting only.

questions.question: What is CSRF?
questions.correctAnswer: An attack that forces the authenticated browser to perform unwanted actions; prevented with CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies.
wrongAnswers: An attack that injects malicious scripts into a page; it is prevented by using innerHTML instead of textContent.
An attack that reads cookies through JavaScript; it is prevented by moving tokens into localStorage.
A CSS rendering flaw; prevented with a CSS reset.

questions.question: What is prototype pollution?
questions.correctAnswer: A vulnerability in which an attacker modifies Object.prototype via keys like __proto__, affecting the entire application.
wrongAnswers: A memory leak caused by long prototype chains that the garbage collector cannot traverse completely.
Having too many methods on a class prototype, causing slowness.
Using prototype-based libraries in a class-based codebase.

questions.question: How does structuredClone work?
questions.correctAnswer: It creates a deep copy of cloneable values (Map, Set, Date, cycles), but doesn't copy functions or class prototypes.
wrongAnswers: It creates a shallow copy of the value and preserves functions, getters and class prototypes, so instances keep their methods.
It serializes the value to JSON and parses it back, so Dates become strings and Maps and Sets are lost in the copy.
It clones DOM elements with their event listeners.

questions.question: What is the Observer pattern?
questions.correctAnswer: Objects (observers) subscribe to a subject and are notified of changes; the basis of events and streams.
wrongAnswers: A pattern that ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global access point to it.
A pattern in which one central object controls the creation and lifecycle of every other object.
A pattern that converts one interface into another.

questions.question: What are the Module pattern and IIFE?
questions.correctAnswer: An IIFE is a function executed immediately, creating a private scope; the Module pattern uses closures to encapsulate state, now replaced by ES Modules.
wrongAnswers: An IIFE is a module imported with import(), and the Module pattern is a CSS methodology for organizing stylesheets by component.
An IIFE is a function that runs on every page navigation, and the Module pattern is the package format used by npm.
Both are synonyms for ES Modules' import/export.

questions.question: What is memoization?
questions.correctAnswer: Caching the results of pure functions based on their arguments, avoiding recalculation.
wrongAnswers: Storing variables in localStorage so their values survive page reloads and browser restarts.
Writing comments to remember what code does.
Limiting how often a function runs per second.

questions.question: How do you deal with decimal number precision?
questions.correctAnswer: Numbers are 64-bit floats (0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3); use integers in cents, toFixed for display or decimal libraries; BigInt for large integers.
wrongAnswers: Call parseInt on every arithmetic result, which removes floating-point errors while keeping the decimal places intact.
Use the native Decimal type introduced in ES2015, which stores exact decimal values for currency calculations.
Use parseInt on every result, which fixes all precision issues.

questions.question: What are Tagged Templates?
questions.correctAnswer: Functions that process template literals (a tag followed by a template literal), used in styled-components and safe SQL.
wrongAnswers: HTML templates marked with data-tag attributes that the browser fills with values from JavaScript objects.
Template literals that are only allowed to contain HTML tags and are escaped automatically when interpolated.
Git tags applied to template files.

questions.question: What are decorators and their current status in JavaScript?
questions.correctAnswer: A standardized proposal for annotating classes and members with @; already supported by transpilers and being implemented in engines.
wrongAnswers: A long-standing native feature supported by every browser since ES2015 and used widely without any transpiler.
A TypeScript-only feature that will never be part of the JavaScript language, so it always requires tsc.
A CSS feature for decorating text.

questions.question: What is the difference between dynamic import() and static import?
questions.correctAnswer: Dynamic import loads modules on demand and returns a Promise, enabling code splitting; static import is resolved before execution.
wrongAnswers: Dynamic import() is synchronous and returns the module object directly, so it can be used anywhere without await.
Static import loads on demand; dynamic import is resolved before execution.
Dynamic import only works in Node; static import only in browsers.

questions.question: What is top-level await?
questions.correctAnswer: It allows using await at the top level of ES modules, without wrapping in an async function.
wrongAnswers: It allows await at the top level of CommonJS files loaded with require, blocking the importer until it resolves.
It makes every function declared in the module async automatically so await can be used anywhere.
It allows await in any CommonJS file.

questions.question: How does type coercion work in [] + {} and [] == ![]?
questions.correctAnswer: Operators convert to primitives: [] + {} results in "[object Object]" and [] == ![] is true, because both become 0. Avoid implicit coercion.
wrongAnswers: [] + {} results in 0 because both operands become numbers, and [] == ![] is false because an array is never equal to a boolean.
[] + {} returns "{}" by concatenating the object's JSON, and [] == ![] is false because the two values have different types.
[] + {} results in 0 and [] == ![] is false.

questions.question: How do you ensure JavaScript code quality in teams?
questions.correctAnswer: ESLint, Prettier, tests (Vitest/Jest), code review, TypeScript/JSDoc and automated CI.
wrongAnswers: Have a single senior developer write and approve all the code so that the style stays consistent without tooling.
Skip tests to ship faster and rely on users reporting bugs in production, fixing them with hotfixes.
Minifying the code so it is harder to change.
